newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kuehbacher doubts Bonn can cut deficit to 2.9 pct.
newsitem.headline: Kuehbacher doubts Bonn can cut deficit to 2.9 pct.

text.p: Bundesbank council member Klaus-Dieter Kuehbacher said on Monday he doubted that the German government would reach its goal of cutting its budget deficit to 2.9 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) in 1997.

Kuehbacher also warned against attempts to use the leeway provided by the Maastricht Treaty for a more generous interpretation of convergence, saying the resulting loss of faith in the planned single currency would cause heavy turbulence on currency and capital markets.

Postponing the launch of the euro, which is scheduled to go ahead on January 1, 1999, would result in a major setback to government efforts to consolidate their budgets, Kuehbacher said according to the text of a speech on monetary union.
Kuehbacher doubts Bonn can cut deficit to 2.9 pct
Therefore starting European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) with a small group of countries appeared to be a sensible option, Kuehbacher said.

"It is likely to be difficult for many countries to qualify for membership," Kuehbacher said, adding that Germany had lost its image as "paragon of stability policy," albeit in part because of the cost of funding unification.
He noted that Germany's budget deficit was 3.8 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) in 1996, well above the three percent limit set by the Maastricht Treaty.
The Treaty allows leeway to overshoot that level in special circumstances. Countries seeking to qualify for monetary union will be judged in early 1998 on the basis of their performance in 1997.
"The finance minister has forecast that the deficit ratio will fall to 2.9 percent in 1997, the relevant year for the decision," Kuehbacher said.

"But I don't believe that this undertaking can succeed in view of the fact that the economic upturn is still not self-sustaining and in view of the continued enormous burden that unemployment is putting on public budgets."
Only tax increases or drastic government spending cuts could still guarantee Germany would meet the deficit criterion, Kuehbacher said.
He noted that inadequate progress on convergence raised the question of whether the criteria should be interpreted more liberally to achieve a launch of monetary union with a large number of members.

"The Maastricht Treaty allows a certain leeway at least with regard to the fiscal criteria. Such an attempt to start monetary union at all costs must be clearly rejected because of the risks to stability this would entail" Kuehbacher said.
If public confidence in the planned euro waned and international financial markets began to doubt its stability, heavy turbulence on currency and capital markets would probably ensue.
"These dangers can only be prevented if the governments and central banks of Europe insisted unshakeably on a strict interpretation of the Maastricht critieria," Kuehbacher said.
Postponement was an option but would take the pressure off states to converge just at a time when it was starting to take effect -- "albeit far too late."
"Against this background I find it extremely doubtful that a postponement of the starting date would be likely to lead to a better development on convergence."
Markets would doubt any new starting dates set and increased market speculation would lead bond yields higher, increasing the interest burden on governments.
"A start with a small circle therefore seems sensible," Kuehbacher said.

A small EMU meant that the overall advantages of EMU -- for example the expected boost to growth resulting from an increase in investment that would result from the absence of currency risk -- would be less significant at first, Kuehbacher said.
But the benefits would grow as more EU members joined monetary union at a later date, Kuehbacher said.
--David Crossland, Frankfurt Newsroom, +49 69 756525
